scenes.title: Menelaus Kills Euphorbus
scenes.summary: Menelaus sees that Patroclus has fallen and bestrides the body like a cow over her first calf. Euphorbus, son of Panthous, who struck Patroclus first, tells him to give up the body and the bloody spoils or lose his life. Menelaus answers that the sons of Panthous are prouder than leopard, lion or boar, and reminds him how his brother Hyperenor scorned him and never went home to his wife and parents. Euphorbus vows to avenge that brother and bring Menelaus' head and armor to his parents, Panthous and Phrontis. His spear bends back on Menelaus' shield; Menelaus prays to Zeus and drives his spear through Euphorbus' neck. The young man falls like an olive sapling uprooted by a storm, his hair, like the Graces', bound with gold and silver, wet with blood. No Trojan dares come against Menelaus, as dogs and herdsmen keep away from a lion devouring a cow.

scenes.title: Menelaus Gives Way to Hector
scenes.summary: Apollo, in the likeness of Mentes, leader of the Cicones, turns Hector from his vain pursuit of Achilles' immortal horses and tells him that Menelaus has killed Euphorbus. Hector, grieving, sees Menelaus stripping the armor and comes through the champions shouting, like the flame of Hephaestus. Menelaus debates with his own heart: if he leaves the armor and Patroclus, the Danaans will blame him; if he fights Hector alone, he will be surrounded; and a man who fights a man whom a god honors brings a great bane on himself. He decides to look for Ajax, and gives ground step by step, turning back again and again, like a bearded lion driven from a farmyard.

scenes.title: Ajax Stands over Patroclus
scenes.summary: Menelaus finds Ajax on the left of the battle and calls him to save at least the naked body, since Hector has the armor. Hector, who has stripped Patroclus, is dragging the body away to cut off the head and give the corpse to the dogs of Troy, when Ajax comes up with his shield like a tower. Hector withdraws to his chariot and sends the armor to the city, to be great fame for him. Ajax stands over the son of Menoetius like a lion over its young, with Menelaus beside him, nursing great grief.

scenes.title: Glaucus Rebukes Hector
scenes.summary: Glaucus, leader of the Lycians, rebukes Hector: his fame is empty, for he left Sarpedon, his guest-friend and companion, to the Argives, and dared not face Ajax. The Lycians will go home unless the Trojans fight; if they drag Patroclus into Troy, the Argives will give back Sarpedon's armor and body. Hector answers that he does not fear battle, but the mind of Zeus is always stronger; let Glaucus stand by him and watch whether he will be a coward all day long.

scenes.title: Hector in the Armor of Achilles
scenes.summary: Hector calls on the Trojans, Lycians and Dardanians to remember their courage while he puts on Achilles' armor. He runs after the men carrying it, changes his armor apart from the battle, and puts on the immortal armor that the gods gave Peleus and Peleus gave his son, who will not grow old in it. Zeus sees him and, shaking his head, speaks to his own heart: Hector does not think of the death that is close to him; he has killed the gentle companion of the best of men and taken his armor against all order, but Zeus will give him great power now, in recompense, since Andromache will never receive the armor from him at his homecoming. Zeus nods and fits the armor to Hector's body; Ares enters him, and he goes among the allies flashing in the armor of the son of Peleus.

scenes.title: Hector Urges the Allies
scenes.summary: Hector goes among the leaders of the allies, Mesthles, Glaucus, Medon, Thersilochus, Asteropaeus, Deisenor, Hippothous, Phorcys, Chromius and Ennomus the augur, and urges them on: he did not gather them for their numbers but to protect the wives and children of the Trojans, and he wears down his own people with gifts and food for them and builds up their spirit. Whoever drags Patroclus among the Trojans and makes Ajax give way will have half the spoils and as much fame as Hector. They charge with spears raised, hoping to drag the body from Ajax, the fools; over it Ajax took the lives of many.

scenes.title: Menelaus Calls the Achaean Leaders
scenes.summary: Ajax tells Menelaus that he fears less for the corpse than for their own heads, now that Hector, a cloud of war, covers everything, and asks him to call the best of the Danaans. Menelaus calls on the leaders who drink at the public cost beside the sons of Atreus to come of their own accord and be indignant that Patroclus should become a plaything for the Trojan dogs. Swift Ajax, son of Oileus, comes first, then Idomeneus and Meriones, and others the narrator cannot name.

scenes.title: The Fight over the Body
scenes.summary: The Trojans come on with a shout like a wave roaring at the mouth of a river. The Achaeans stand around Patroclus fenced with their shields, and Zeus pours mist about their helmets, since he had not hated Patroclus while he lived and would not let him become a prey for the Trojan dogs. The Trojans push the Achaeans back and drag at the body, but Ajax, in looks and deeds the best after Achilles, rallies them and scatters the Trojans like a wild boar scattering dogs and young men. He kills Hippothous, son of Lethus the Pelasgian, who had tied a strap to Patroclus' ankle and was dragging him by the foot; Hector's spear misses Ajax and kills Schedius, leader of the Phocians; Ajax kills Phorcys, son of Phaenops, as he stands over Hippothous. The Achaeans drag away the dead and strip them.

scenes.title: Apollo Rouses Aeneas
scenes.summary: The Trojans would have been driven back into Ilios and the Argives would have won glory even beyond the portion of Zeus, had not Apollo, in the likeness of the herald Periphas, son of Epytus, rebuked Aeneas: other men have saved their cities by their own strength, and Zeus wills victory for the Trojans, yet they tremble and do not fight. Aeneas knows the god, calls on Hector and the leaders, and the Trojans stand again. Aeneas kills Leiocritus, companion of Lycomedes; Lycomedes kills the Paeonian Apisaon; Asteropaeus charges but cannot break through, for Ajax has the Achaeans stand close around the body behind their shields and fight at close quarters. The earth is wet with blood, but fewer Achaeans die, since they defend one another.

scenes.title: Mist over the Body
scenes.summary: Around the body the best men fight in mist, so that sun and moon seem lost, while the rest of the armies fight at their ease under a clear sky, keeping apart. Thrasymedes and Antilochus, fighting apart as Nestor had ordered, do not yet know that Patroclus is dead. All day long the two sides pull the body this way and that in a narrow space, as men stretch a bull's hide soaked in fat, and Ares and Athena themselves could not find fault with the fighting. Achilles does not know that Patroclus is dead, for the battle is far off under the wall of Troy, and his mother has not told him this evil. One Achaean says it would be better for the earth to gape for them all than to let the Trojans drag the body away; a Trojan says that no one must hang back, even if they all must die beside it. The iron din goes up to the bronze sky.

scenes.title: The Horses of Achilles Weep
scenes.summary: Achilles' horses stand apart from the battle weeping for their charioteer. Automedon cannot move them with whip, soothing words or threats; they stand fixed like a pillar on a tomb, heads bowed to the ground, hot tears falling, their manes soiled in the dust. Zeus pities them and speaks to his own heart: why did the gods give immortal horses to Peleus, a mortal, to share the sorrows of men, the most miserable of all that breathe and creep upon the earth? Hector will not ride behind them; Zeus breathes might into them so that they carry Automedon safe to the ships, for he will still give the Trojans glory to kill until the sun goes down. The horses shake the dust from their manes and carry the chariot into the battle.

scenes.title: Automedon and Alcimedon
scenes.summary: Automedon, grieving for Patroclus, swoops through the battle with the horses like a vulture among geese, but alone in the chariot he cannot both drive and strike. Alcimedon rebukes him for fighting alone, and Automedon gives him the whip and reins and gets down to fight. Hector sees the horses with what he takes for poor charioteers and sets out with Aeneas, Chromius and Aretus to take them. Automedon prays to Zeus, tells Alcimedon to keep the horses breathing on his back, and calls the Ajaxes and Menelaus. His spear kills Aretus, who falls like an ox struck behind the horns; Hector's spear misses him. The Ajaxes part them before they fight with swords, and Automedon strips Aretus, saying that he has eased his heart a little for Patroclus, though the man was a lesser one, and mounts the chariot bloody like a lion that has eaten a bull.

scenes.title: Athena and Apollo
scenes.summary: Zeus' mind turns, and Athena comes down wrapped in a purple cloud, like a rainbow Zeus stretches out as a portent of war or storm. In the likeness of Phoenix she tells Menelaus that it would be a shame if the dogs tore Achilles' trusted companion under the wall of Troy. Menelaus answers that he would defend Patroclus if Athena gave him strength, but Hector has the might of fire. Glad to have been prayed to first, Athena puts strength in his shoulders and knees and the daring of a fly in his breast. He kills Podes, son of Eetion, Hector's dear companion at the feast, and drags the body away. Apollo, in the likeness of Phaenops, son of Asius, taunts Hector for shrinking from Menelaus, once a soft spearman; a black cloud of grief covers Hector, and he goes through the champions. Zeus takes up the aegis, covers Ida in clouds, thunders and lightens, and gives victory to the Trojans.

scenes.title: The Achaeans Routed
scenes.summary: Peneleos the Boeotian is the first to flee, his shoulder grazed to the bone by Polydamas' spear. Hector stabs Leitus, son of Alectryon, on the wrist, and he leaves the fight. Idomeneus' spear snaps at the socket on Hector's corselet; Hector's spear misses Idomeneus and kills Coeranus of Lyctus, Meriones' charioteer, who had driven up to save Idomeneus. Meriones picks up the reins and tells Idomeneus to drive to the ships, and he flees in fear.

scenes.title: Ajax's Prayer for Light
scenes.summary: Ajax sees that Zeus is helping the Trojans: their missiles all strike home, while the Achaeans' fall in vain. He tells Menelaus that they must plan both to save the body and to come back alive, and that someone should tell Achilles that his companion is dead, but the mist hides everyone. He prays to Zeus to free the Achaeans from the mist and destroy them, if he must, in the light. Zeus pities his tears and scatters the mist, and the whole battle is seen. Ajax tells Menelaus to look for Antilochus and send him to Achilles.

scenes.title: Antilochus Sent to Achilles
scenes.summary: Menelaus goes unwillingly from the body, like a lion leaving a farmyard at dawn, and charges the Ajaxes and Meriones to remember the gentleness of Patroclus, who was kind to all while he lived. He looks everywhere like an eagle, which they say has the sharpest sight of all birds, and finds Antilochus on the left of the battle. He tells him that Patroclus, the best of the Achaeans, is dead, and bids him run to Achilles so that he may save the naked body. Antilochus is struck speechless, his eyes fill with tears, but he gives his armor to Laodocus and runs weeping to bring Achilles the evil news.

scenes.title: The Body Carried from the Battle
scenes.summary: Menelaus leaves the Pylians to Thrasymedes and returns to the Ajaxes. Achilles, he says, cannot fight without armor; they must save the body and themselves. Ajax tells Menelaus and Meriones to lift the body while the two Ajaxes, of one name and one spirit, hold off the Trojans. The Trojans charge like dogs at a wounded boar but scatter when the Ajaxes turn on them. The war burns around the bearers like a fire in a city, and they carry the body like mules dragging a beam down a mountain path, while the Ajaxes hold back the Trojans like a wooded ridge holding back the streams of mighty rivers. Hector and Aeneas press on, and the young Achaeans flee before them like starlings and jackdaws before a falcon, dropping much armor around the ditch; there is no respite from the war.

days.label: Day 26
days.note: The third day of battle continues (11.1 to 18.242). The book has no mark of the hour: around the body the fighters are covered in mist while the rest of the battle goes on under a clear sun (17.366–377), until Zeus scatters the mist at Ajax's prayer (17.645–650). Zeus has promised the Trojans glory to kill until the sun goes down (17.453–455); the sun sets at 18.239–242.
